title: Comparing numbers stored as strings
question: Prices read from a CSV file are still text. A program picks the largest of "10", "9" and "100" with a max function that compares the values as strings, and it returns "9". Why?
options: Strings compare character by character, and "9" > "1"
max returns the first item when it is given only strings
Strings are ranked by length, and shorter ones rank higher
Each string is compared by the sum of its character codes
explanation: String comparison is lexicographic: characters are compared one at a time by their code, so "9" against "10" is decided by "9" against "1", and "9" is greater before length ever matters. Position and length play no part, and summing character codes would make "100" the largest. Convert the values to numbers before comparing them.

title: The slow end of a singly linked list
question: A singly linked list keeps references to both its head and its tail node, and each node has only a next pointer. Which operation still takes O(n)?
options: Inserting a new node at the head
Appending a new node after the tail
Removing the current head node
Removing the current tail node
explanation: Removing the tail means making the node before it the new tail and clearing its next, and with only next pointers the one way to find that node is to walk from the head: O(n). Inserting at the head, removing the head and appending after the tail only touch references you already hold, so each is O(1). That is why a singly linked list with a tail pointer works well as a queue (add at the tail, remove at the head), while cheap removal at both ends needs a doubly linked list.

title: A data structure for undo
question: A text editor records every edit so that each press of Undo reverts the most recent edit that has not been undone yet. Which data structure fits the undo history?
options: A queue: add each edit at the back, undo from the front
A stack: push each edit, pop one on every Undo
A hash set of edits keyed by their edit ID
An array sorted by edit size, largest first
explanation: Undo is last in, first out: the edit made last is the first one reverted, which is exactly push and pop on a stack, both O(1). A queue would revert the oldest edit first. A hash set has no order at all, and sorting by size ignores when each edit happened. Many editors add a second stack for Redo, onto which each undone edit is pushed.

title: Bracket checker that accepts '(()'
options: It should push closing brackets and pop opening ones
It pops before checking that the stack is non-empty
It ignores openers still left on the stack at the end
It compares each closer with the bottom of the stack, not the top
explanation: A string is balanced only if every closer matches the most recent opener and nothing is left open at the end. Here the ')' matches the second '(', but the first '(' is still on the stack when the loop ends and the function returns True without looking. The fix is return not stack. The empty-stack check already runs before pop() thanks to short-circuit evaluation, and list.pop() takes the top, the last opener pushed.

title: Holding jobs for a shared printer
question: An office printer receives jobs from many people and must print them in the order they arrived. How should the pending jobs be stored?
options: In a queue: add new jobs at the back, take the next from the front
In a stack: push new jobs, then pop the next one from the top
In a list sorted by page count, smallest job first
In a queue: add new jobs at the front, take the next from the front
explanation: First come, first served is FIFO, which is what a queue gives: enqueue at the back and dequeue from the front, both O(1) with a proper queue such as collections.deque. Adding and removing at the same end is LIFO, that is a stack, so the last job sent would print first and early jobs could wait indefinitely. Sorting by page count is a scheduling policy that breaks arrival order.

title: A comparator that subtracts
options: List.sort is not stable; use Collections.sort to keep the order
a - b can overflow int and flip its sign; use Integer.compare(a, b)
Comparators must return only -1, 0 or 1; clamp a - b to that range
The lambda compares Integer references; cast both to int first
explanation: A comparator only needs the sign of its result, but a - b is computed in 32-bit int: 2,000,000,000 - (-2,000,000,000) = 4,000,000,000 wraps around to a negative number, so the comparator claims the larger value is the smaller one. Integer.compare(a, b), or Comparator.naturalOrder(), compares without subtracting and cannot overflow. Any negative, zero or positive result is allowed, so -1/0/1 is not required; the subtraction unboxes both values, so no references are compared; and List.sort is stable for objects (Collections.sort just delegates to it).

title: Binary search that skips the last candidate
options: Loop while lo <= hi, so a range of one element is still checked
Compute mid as (lo + hi + 1) // 2, so mid rounds up instead
Set lo = mid instead of lo = mid + 1 when a[mid] < target
Return lo instead of -1 once the loop ends without a match
explanation: With hi = len(a) - 1 the range [lo, hi] is inclusive, so when lo == hi it still holds one unchecked element; while lo < hi stops before testing it, and a target in that last slot is never compared. while lo <= hi fixes it. Rounding mid up does not help when the loop never runs, lo = mid can loop forever (search([1, 3], 3) would repeat mid = 0), and returning lo reports an index even for values that are absent.

title: First occurrence among duplicates
question: A sorted array of timestamps has duplicates, such as [1, 2, 4, 4, 4, 7]. A plain binary search for 4 may stop at any matching index, but you need the first one, in O(log n) even if a value repeats a million times. Which change does that?
options: On a match, step left one index at a time until the value changes
On a match, record mid and continue right (lo = mid + 1)
Search for target - 1 instead and return the index right after it
On a match, record mid and continue left (hi = mid - 1)
explanation: Recording the match and continuing with hi = mid - 1 keeps halving the range until no earlier copy can exist; the last recorded index is the first occurrence, and the cost stays O(log n). Stepping left after a hit degrades to O(n) when the value repeats many times, continuing right finds the last occurrence instead, and searching for target - 1 fails whenever that value is not in the array. Python's bisect_left returns the same leftmost position.

title: A reversal that changes nothing
question:
a = [1, 2, 3, 4]
for i in range(len(a)):
    j = len(a) - 1 - i
    a[i], a[j] = a[j], a[i]
print(a)

What is printed, and why?
options: [4, 3, 2, 1], since every pair is swapped exactly once
[4, 2, 3, 1], since only the outer pair is swapped
[1, 2, 3, 4], as the later steps undo the swaps
IndexError, since j becomes negative in the last step
explanation: The indices i and j walk towards each other, but the loop keeps going after they cross: i = 0 and 1 reverse the list to [4, 3, 2, 1], then i = 2 and 3 swap the same pairs again and restore [1, 2, 3, 4]. j only goes down to 0, so nothing raises. Stop when the pointers meet, with for i in range(len(a) // 2) or while i < j, or simply call a.reverse().
